title: From Zombie Fungi to Toothless Birds: How David Attenborough's Legacy Lives on in Species Names
summary: Deep in a dark cave, an orb-weaving spider is no longer in control. A parasitic fungus called *Gibellula attenboroughii* has hijacked its nervous system, forcing the arachnid to abandon its hiding spot and march toward the cave entrance. There, the spider dies, and the fungus erupts from its body, releasing spores to infect new victims. This macabre manipulation is just one reason scientists named the newly discovered species after Sir David Attenborough, who turned 100 on May 8. Attenborough's documentaries have shaped how millions see the natural world. For many researchers, his voice was the spark that ignited their careers. "I most likely wouldn't be in the natural sciences if it weren't for David Attenborough's documentaries," said a paleontologist who helped name a 120-million-year-old toothless bird *Imparavis attenboroughi*—"Attenborough's strange bird." The fossil, found in China, pushed back the timeline for toothlessness in this group of proto-birds by 48 million years. About 50 organisms now carry Attenborough's name or legacy. They range from an orchid to a marine worm to one of the earliest known predators. One of the newest is a three-inch-long iridescent bloodworm, *Marphysa davidattenboroughi*, discovered off the coast of Australia. "They're not the most beautiful animals on Earth, but they are important," says taxonomist Nicolas Lavesque, who named it. Lavesque even received a handwritten reply from Attenborough, sending his children into a frenzy of excitement. These eponyms are more than tributes—they're a testament to how one person's passion can ripple across generations, inspiring discoveries that deepen our understanding of life on Earth.
why_it_matters: This story shows how one person's lifelong dedication to sharing nature can spark a continuing cycle of discovery, enriching humanity's understanding of Earth's biodiversity and the importance of conservation.

background_read: Sir David Attenborough (born 1926) is a British broadcaster and naturalist who pioneered wildlife documentary series such as 'Life on Earth' (1979). His distinctive narration has educated millions about nature.
Scientists naming new species after notable individuals is a tradition dating back to Carl Linnaeus; many creatures honor researchers, patrons, or public figures.
The fungus Gibellula attenboroughii belongs to a group of 'zombie fungi' (like Ophiocordyceps) that manipulate insect behavior to spread spores—a phenomenon famously revealed in the genus Cordyceps.

The fossil bird Imparavis attenboroughi, found in Cretaceous rocks in China, represents an early enantiornithine, a group of toothed birds that lived alongside dinosaurs; its lack of teeth suggests convergent evolution with modern birds.

perspectives.description: Eponymous namings celebrate scientific heroes and inspire future generations to pursue fields like biology and paleontology, connecting the public to discoveries.
Some argue that naming species after celebrities can trivialize taxonomy and distract from objective classification; naming rights may overshadow the species' own ecological significance.
The practice of eponyms reflects a historical pattern where science uses human figures to make abstract discoveries relatable, though it can introduce bias or fleeting fame.
As biodiversity declines, future species names might increasingly serve as conservation memorials, emphasizing the urgency to protect habitats before organisms go extinct unnamed.
